title: Him, her, them
description: Say who an action is for, without repeating the noun.
grammarNote: The object pronoun goes before the verb: lo veo, la escucho.

explanation.summary: The direct object is the thing an action happens to. When you have already mentioned it, Spanish replaces it with a pronoun instead of repeating the noun.

sections.heading: The five
sections.body: Me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las. Lo and la replace a thing: lo veo, I see it. La and lo are the same word in meaning when there is no noun to tell them apart, so you use la for a feminine object and lo for a masculine one, or either for a thing whose gender you do not know.

sections.heading: Where it goes
sections.body: The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb: lo veo, no veo lo. With the infinitive, the pronoun goes after it and is attached to it: verlo, quiero verlo. With a gerund it goes before: lo estoy viendo. And a pronoun that is attached to the infinitive or the gerund turns into se: bañarse, I'm washing myself. You will meet that form in B1/6.

examples.en: I am going to get it.

sections.heading: The one that is easy to miss
sections.body: The pronouns lo and la are also the words for the neuter article, and Spanish uses them in a lot of fixed phrases where there is no object at all: lo bueno, the good part; lo mismo, the same; lo de siempre, the usual.

items.note: You, singular. It goes before the verb: te veo.
It, him or it. It takes the place of a masculine object.
It, her. It takes the place of a feminine object.
Us. It goes before the verb: nos ve.
You, plural. It is used in Spain.
An infinitive ending in -ar: entro, entras, entra.
Its forms are irregular: salgo, sales, sale.

drills.note: The object pronoun goes before the verb.
With an infinitive the pronoun goes after it and is attached.
With a gerund the pronoun goes before.

drills.meaning: I see them, they are my friends.

drills.note: Me llamo, and the pronoun is attached to the verb.
